claim: The TwinsUK cohort consists of 765 LCL samples from female Caucasian adult twins, including 134 monozygotic (MZ) twin pairs and 192 dizygotic (DZ) pairs.
source: We searched for v-eQTL in a dataset of 765 LCL samples from female Caucasian adult twins in the TwinsUK cohort, including 134 monozygotic (MZ) twin pairs and 192 dizygotic (DZ) pairs.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the sample composition of the TwinsUK cohort used in the study.

claim: Expression levels of 13,660 genes were determined using whole transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq).
source: The level of expression of 13,660 genes was determined using whole transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of genes analyzed and the method used.

claim: 497 SNPs were identified as peak v-eQTL for 508 genes at FDR < 0.05.
source: Using a non-parametric association test between SNPs within a cis window of ±1 Mbp around the TSS and the square of the residuals ('Materials and methods'), we identified 497 SNPs as peak v-eQTL for 508 genes (false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1A), 23 reaching Bonferroni significance (nominal p-value <8.9 × 10−10).
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of v-eQTL with specific statistical thresholds.

claim: 23 v-eQTL reached Bonferroni significance with nominal p-value < 8.9 × 10−10.
source: Using a non-parametric association test between SNPs within a cis window of ±1 Mbp around the TSS and the square of the residuals ('Materials and methods'), we identified 497 SNPs as peak v-eQTL for 508 genes (false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1A), 23 reaching Bonferroni significance (nominal p-value <8.9 × 10−10).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of v-eQTL meeting Bonferroni significance threshold.

claim: 9.3% of v-eQTL are within 10 kb of the transcription start site.
source: Many of the FDR defined v-eQTL cluster close to the TSS (9.3% are within 10 kb) but they are found at all positions in the window (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage and references Figure 1B showing the distribution.

claim: 181 of the 508 v-eQTL are also significant eQTL at FDR of 0.05.
source: Of the 508 v-eQTL, 181 are also significant eQTL at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.05 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the overlap between v-eQTL and eQTL.

claim: 256 independent SNPs were identified in epistasis with peak v-eQTL for 173 genes at Bonferroni significance (p-value < 1.98 × 10−8).
source: A forward stepwise analysis identified independent examples of epistasis, not induced by linkage disequilibrium; a statistical test was applied to remove signals related to dominance ('Materials and methods'). This identified 256 independent SNPs in apparent epistasis with the peak v-eQTL for 173 genes (Bonferroni, p-value <1.98 × 10−8; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of epistatic interactions with specific statistical thresholds.

claim: The GEUVADIS replication cohort consists of 462 samples with LCL RNA-seq data from 1000 Genomes samples.
source: We replicated our scan for v-eQTL and epistatic interactions in 462 samples with LCL RNA-seq data from 1000 Genomes samples collected by the GEUVADIS consortium (Lappalainen et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the replication cohort size and source.

claim: Of the 23 Bonferroni-significant v-eQTL, 16 replicated in the GEUVADIS cohort at FDR < 0.05.
source: For the 23 v-eQTL that are significant using the Bonferroni threshold, 16 are significant in the GEUVADIS cohort (FDR <0.05), 15 with same direction of effect.
evidence: The manuscript reports replication results with specific numbers and statistical thresholds.

claim: Of the 508 v-eQTL, 28 replicated in the GEUVADIS cohort with FDR < 0.05.
source: Of the 508 v-eQTL, 28 replicated with an FDR <0.05, 26 with same direction of effect.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the replication rate for v-eQTL.

claim: Of the 256 epistasis associations, 246 had information available in the GEUVADIS data.
source: Of the 256 epistasis associations, information on both the SNP and the gene was available for 246 in the GEUVADIS data.
evidence: The manuscript states how many epistasis associations could be tested in replication.

claim: 137 of 246 epistasis associations replicated in GEUVADIS with FDR < 0.05.
source: We found that 137 replicated with FDR <0.05, 131 of which had the same direction of effect (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of replicated epistasis associations.

claim: p-value enrichment analysis indicated replication evidence for 71% of the 246 epistasis associations.
source: p-value enrichment analysis (Storey, 2002) indicated that there was replication evidence for 71% of the 246.
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of p-value enrichment analysis with citation to the method.

claim: A correlation of 0.58 was observed between effect sizes of interactions in both datasets (p-value = 5.9 × 10−24).
source: Moreover, we observed a correlation of 0.58 between the effect sizes of the interactions in both datasets (p-value = 5.9 × 10−24), with 202 of the 246 interactions sharing the same direction of effect (p-value = 2.2 × 10−25) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation statistics between discovery and replication cohorts.

claim: 202 of 246 interactions shared the same direction of effect (p-value = 2.2 × 10−25).
source: Moreover, we observed a correlation of 0.58 between the effect sizes of the interactions in both datasets (p-value = 5.9 × 10−24), with 202 of the 246 interactions sharing the same direction of effect (p-value = 2.2 × 10−25) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the consistency of effect directions across cohorts.

claim: 57 epistasis signals remained significant after controlling for all possible eQTL effects.
source: We then tested whether the epistatic interaction was still significant in models incorporating each eQTL individually at the same threshold as previously applied. Fifty seven epistasis signals remain significant.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of epistasis signals surviving conditional analysis.

claim: The replicated epistatic interactions explain on average 4.3% of phenotypic variance.
source: Using RNA-sequence data from lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) from the TwinsUK cohort, we identify a candidate set of 508 variance associated SNPs. Exploiting the twin design we show that GxE plays a role in ∼70% of these associations. Further investigation of these loci reveals 57 epistatic interactions that replicated in a smaller dataset, explaining on average 4.3% of phenotypic variance.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the average variance explained by replicated interactions.

claim: In 24 cases, more variance is explained by the interaction than by additive contributions.
source: In 24 cases, more variance is explained by the interaction than their additive contributions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of cases where interaction effects exceed additive effects.

claim: GxE plays a role in approximately 70% of the variance associations.
source: Using RNA-sequence data from lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) from the TwinsUK cohort, we identify a candidate set of 508 variance associated SNPs. Exploiting the twin design we show that GxE plays a role in ∼70% of these associations.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the proportion of v-eQTL with GxE evidence.

claim: Up to 16% of variance in gene expression was explained by considering the interaction between variants.
source: We estimated the proportion of variance explained by the interaction in the GEUVADIS cohort to avoid over-estimating effects because of winner's curse. As a result, we were able to determine that up to 16% of the variance in gene expression was explained by considering the interaction between the variants, with an average additional variance explained of 4.3% (Table 2; Supplementary file 1B; Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the maximum variance explained by interactions.

claim: For eight genes with multiple independent interactions with the v-eQTL, up to 10.4% of variance was explained by these multiple interactions.
source: For the eight genes for which we replicated independent interactions with the v-eQTL, we found that in total up to 10.4% of the variance was explained by these multiple interactions, with an average of 5.1%.
evidence: The manuscript reports cumulative variance explained by multiple interactions for specific genes.

claim: For 24 out of 57 replicated examples of epistasis, the interaction explains more variance than the additive effects of the SNPs.
source: For 24 out of 57 the replicated examples of epistasis, the interaction explains more variance than the additive effects of the SNPs.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cases where interaction effects dominate.

claim: The v-eQTL for TRIT1 (rs3131691) lies on the boundary of an ENCODE defined LCL weak enhancer upstream of the gene.
source: The v-eQTL (rs3131691) for TRIT1 lies on the boundary of an ENCODE defined LCL weak enhancer (Dunham et al., 2012; Rosenbloom et al., 2013) upstream of the gene, while the SNP in epistasis (rs230273) lies on the boundary of a downstream LCL enhancer region (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic location of the v-eQTL relative to regulatory elements with citations.

claim: The epistasis SNP for TRIT1 (rs230273) lies on the boundary of a downstream LCL enhancer region.
source: The v-eQTL (rs3131691) for TRIT1 lies on the boundary of an ENCODE defined LCL weak enhancer (Dunham et al., 2012; Rosenbloom et al., 2013) upstream of the gene, while the SNP in epistasis (rs230273) lies on the boundary of a downstream LCL enhancer region (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic location of the epistasis SNP relative to regulatory elements.

claim: The TRIT1 v-eQTL is 28 bp upstream of a strong eQTL signal (rs34387655).
source: The v-eQTL is also 28 bp upstream of a strong eQTL signal (rs34387655).
evidence: The manuscript states the distance between the v-eQTL and a nearby eQTL.

claim: The eQTL rs34387655 has minor allele frequency (MAF) 0.08.
source: This eQTL has minor allele frequency (MAF) 0.08, and is in high D′ with the v-eQTL (MAF = 0.30), suggesting that the eQTL could be a recent mutation co-segregating with one allele of the v-eQTL.
evidence: The manuscript reports the MAF of the eQTL.

claim: The v-eQTL rs3131691 has MAF = 0.30.
source: This eQTL has minor allele frequency (MAF) 0.08, and is in high D′ with the v-eQTL (MAF = 0.30), suggesting that the eQTL could be a recent mutation co-segregating with one allele of the v-eQTL.
evidence: The manuscript reports the MAF of the v-eQTL.

claim: The eQTL rs34387655 is in high D′ with the v-eQTL rs3131691.
source: This eQTL has minor allele frequency (MAF) 0.08, and is in high D′ with the v-eQTL (MAF = 0.30), suggesting that the eQTL could be a recent mutation co-segregating with one allele of the v-eQTL.
evidence: The manuscript reports the linkage disequilibrium measure between the two SNPs.

claim: The TRIT1 interaction remained significant when analyzing only major allele homozygotes for the eQTL (p-value = 0.0095).
source: But this eQTL cannot explain the observed interaction, which was still significant when analyzing only major allele homozygotes for the eQTL (p-value = 0.0095).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of conditional analysis to rule out confounding.

claim: No trans SNPs in epistasis with v-eQTL replicated in the GEUVADIS cohort.
source: The discussion up to this point concerns SNPs in cis with the expressed gene. Looking for examples of trans SNPs (>5 Mbp from the TSS) in epistasis with the v-eQTL yielded no hits that replicated in the GEUVADIS cohort.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of replicated trans epistasis.

claim: For 15 of 273 v-eQTL genes, interactions between cis and trans regions explain more than 10% of variance in expression.
source: We had information about the IBD sharing around 273 of the 508 v-eQTL genes. For 15 of these, interactions between the cis and trans regions explain more than 10% of the variance in expression.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of heritability analysis using twin data.

claim: For 9 of the 15 genes with cis-trans interactions, the interaction effect was more than the estimated combined direct genetic contribution of both cis and trans variants.
source: For all of these there is greater evidence of cis-trans epistasis affecting expression than an influence of common environment, and for 9 of the 15 the interaction effect was more than the estimated combined direct genetic contribution of both cis and trans variants (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the comparison of interaction effects to additive effects in heritability analysis.

claim: Using MZ twin data, it is estimated that 70% of v-eQTL also act as discordant eQTL (d-eQTL).
source: Using our MZ data, we have tested our 508 v-eQTL for evidence that they are also d-eQTL; using the methods from Storey (2002) we estimate that 70% of the v-eQTL act in this manner.
evidence: The manuscript reports the estimated proportion of v-eQTL with GxE evidence using a specific method.

claim: 176 of the 508 v-eQTL show significant effects on discordance at FDR < 0.05.
source: In total, 176 of the 508 v-eQTL show significant effects on discordance (FDR <0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of v-eQTL with significant discordance effects.

claim: Of the 176 v-eQTL with discordance effects, 40.3% are estimated to also be eQTL.
source: Of these 176, we estimate the proportion that are also eQTL as 40.3%, less than the proportion of all v-eQTL which act as eQTL.
evidence: The manuscript reports the estimated overlap between d-eQTL and eQTL.

claim: Epistasis is defined statistically as a joint effect of two loci on a trait, significant beyond the sum of additive effects.
source: Here, we focus on the discovery and characterisation of epistasis, by which we mean that the effect of a genetic variant on a trait depends on the genotype at one or more other locations in the genome. Statistically we define this as a joint effect of two loci on a trait, significant beyond the sum of additive effects.
evidence: The manuscript provides an explicit statistical definition of epistasis used in the study.

claim: Epistasis plays an important role in evolution on long time frames.
source: On long time frames, epistasis plays an important role in evolution (Breen et al., 2012), and has been used to explain the persistence of deleterious mutations under selection (Hemani et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature supporting the evolutionary role of epistasis.

claim: Epistasis has been used to explain the persistence of deleterious mutations under selection.
source: On long time frames, epistasis plays an important role in evolution (Breen et al., 2012), and has been used to explain the persistence of deleterious mutations under selection (Hemani et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the role of epistasis in maintaining deleterious mutations.

claim: Huang et al. (2012) found little concordance between genetic variants associated with three traits in two distinct Drosophila populations.
source: Huang et al. (2012) looked at mapping variants associated with three traits in two distinct Drosophila populations and found very little concordance between the results.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing population-specific genetic effects in Drosophila.

claim: Bloom et al. (2013) discovered 78 pairs of loci in epistasis affecting 24 traits in yeast crosses.
source: In a study of sources of variation in yeast crosses, Bloom et al. (2013) carried out a scan for epistasis which discovered 78 pairs of loci where the effect of one was dependent on the genotype of the other, affecting 24 traits.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study reporting epistasis in yeast.

claim: In the yeast study by Bloom et al. (2013), the median variance explained by epistatic interactions was 3%.
source: In most cases these interactions explained little of the genetic variation in trait, the median was 3%, but in one case 14% of this variance was explained.
evidence: The manuscript cites specific variance explained values from the yeast epistasis study.

claim: In one case in the Bloom et al. (2013) yeast study, 14% of variance was explained by epistasis.
source: In most cases these interactions explained little of the genetic variation in trait, the median was 3%, but in one case 14% of this variance was explained.
evidence: The manuscript cites the maximum variance explained by epistasis in the yeast study.

claim: Significant interactions between variants have been observed to affect rice yields.
source: Significant interactions between variants have also been seen to affect rice yields (Huang et al., 2014) and metabolic traits in yeast (Wentzell et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on epistasis in rice.

claim: Significant interactions between variants have been observed to affect metabolic traits in yeast.
source: Significant interactions between variants have also been seen to affect rice yields (Huang et al., 2014) and metabolic traits in yeast (Wentzell et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on epistasis affecting yeast metabolism.

claim: Epistasis has proved harder to identify in human genome-wide association studies compared to model organisms.
source: However, epistasis has proved harder to identify in human genome-wide association studies. In particular, with classical complex traits there has not been evidence of epistasis on the scale seen in model organisms.
evidence: The manuscript states the difficulty of detecting epistasis in human studies.

claim: The difficulty in detecting epistasis in humans may be partly due to the large number of possible interactions to test in the human genome.
source: This may be in part because of the large number of possible interactions to test in the human genome, and possibly because the genetic architecture is different in a homogeneous outbred population from that of a cross between inbred lines.
evidence: The manuscript provides potential explanations for the difficulty in detecting epistasis in humans.

claim: Paré et al. (2010) described how an interaction, either genetic or environmental, can induce genotype dependent variance in phenotypes.
source: Paré et al. (2010) have described how an interaction, either genetic or environmental, can induce genotype dependent variance in phenotypes.
evidence: The manuscript cites the theoretical basis for using variance QTL to detect interactions.

claim: Paré et al. (2010) suggested that SNPs showing variance effects could be prioritized in the search for interactions.
source: They suggested that SNPs which showed such effects on variance could be prioritized in the search for interactions.
evidence: The manuscript cites the methodological approach proposed by Paré et al.

claim: Yang et al. (2012) identified one replicated variance QTL locus for height and BMI in approximately 150,000 samples.
source: Previous work that looked for variance QTL for height and BMI in ∼150,000 samples identified one replicated locus (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on variance QTL for complex traits.

claim: Wang et al. (2014) looked at v-eQTL in gene expression in the TwinsUK cohort using microarrays.
source: Wang et al. (2014) also looked at v-eQTL in gene expression in the same cohort as presented here, where expression was quantified using microarrays rather than sequence based technology (Grundberg et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on v-eQTL in the same cohort using different technology.

claim: Wang et al. (2014) concluded that v-eQTL can often be induced by partial linkage disequilibrium with eQTL.
source: They concluded that v-eQTL can often be induced by partial linkage disequilibrium with eQTL.
evidence: The manuscript cites the conclusions of Wang et al. regarding v-eQTL mechanisms.

claim: Wang et al. (2014) discovered differences in expression between monozygotic twins that were dependent on genotype of the twin pair.
source: They also discovered differences in expression between monozygotic twins which were dependent on genotype of the twin pair, such differences cannot be induced by these partial linkages and thus point to a gene–environment interaction.
evidence: The manuscript cites evidence for GxE from Wang et al.

claim: Wang et al. (2014) concluded that epistasis is not a cause of v-eQTL.
source: The haplotype effect explanation for v-eQTL, combined with a literature which has concluded in many cases epistasis does not contribute to variation in complex traits (Hill et al., 2008), led them to conclude epistasis is not a cause of v-eQTL.
evidence: The manuscript cites the conclusions of Wang et al. regarding epistasis and v-eQTL.

claim: Microarray data are less suitable than RNA-seq for detecting v-eQTL because saturation of signal limits discrimination at extremes.
source: We note that microarray data are also less suitable than RNA-seq for the purpose of detecting v-eQTL, because saturation of signal limits discrimination at extremes (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites technical limitations of microarrays for variance analysis.

claim: Neither Yang et al. (2012) nor Wang et al. (2014) used variance QTL directly to identify epistatic or GxE interactions.
source: In neither Yang et al. (2012) nor Wang et al. (2014) were variance QTL directly used to identify epistatic or GxE interactions.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts previous work with the current study's approach.

claim: Ansel et al. (2008) and Jimenez-Gomez et al. (2011) used the coefficient of variance within inbred lines to map variants controlling stochastic influence in phenotypic variation.
source: Two papers have also looked at producing a phenotype related to variance, in both cases using the coefficient of variance (CV) within inbred lines to map variants which control the stochastic influence in phenotypic variation (Ansel et al., 2008; Jimenez-Gomez et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on variance-related phenotypes in model organisms.

claim: Standard eQTL working on mean gene expression levels can be mistaken for having variance effects in the presence of a mean–variance relationship.
source: There are two other mechanisms by which genotype dependent variance can be induced. Firstly, as Sun et al. (2013) have described, standard eQTL working on mean gene expression levels can be mistaken for having variance effects in the presence of a mean–variance relationship.
evidence: The manuscript cites a potential confounding factor in v-eQTL detection.

claim: With RNA-seq data, a square root transformation breaks the link between mean and variance.
source: With RNA-seq data, the relationship between mean and variance is clear; as RNA-seq reads are sampled from a Poisson distribution, a square root transformation breaks this link.
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical approach to handle mean-variance relationships in RNA-seq data.

claim: Haplotype effects can appear as v-eQTL when a recent strong eQTL co-segregates with a more common SNP.
source: Secondly, as discussed by the Wang et al. (2014) paper described above, haplotype effects can appear as v-eQTL. For example, the situation where a recent strong eQTL co-segregates with a more common SNP (i.e., the SNP is in low R2 with the eQTL, but high D′) could be observed as variance effects of a single SNP.
evidence: The manuscript describes another potential confounding mechanism for v-eQTL.

claim: Haplotype effects could be mistaken for epistasis between two variants which jointly tag the eQTL.
source: This could also by mistaken for epistasis between two variants which jointly tag the eQTL.
evidence: The manuscript describes how haplotype effects could confound epistasis detection.

claim: The study controls for haplotype effects by explicitly considering all possible explanatory eQTL in the full sequence data available for the replication sample.
source: We control for this possibility by explicitly considering all possible explanatory eQTL in the full sequence data available for our replication sample.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodological approach to rule out haplotype confounding.

claim: Samples were genotyped on a combination of HumanHap300, HumanHap610Q, 1 M-Duo and 1.2MDuo 1M Illumina arrays.
source: Samples were genotyped on a combination of the HumanHap300, HumanHap610Q, 1 M-Duo and 1.2MDuo 1M Illumnia arrays.
evidence: The manuscript describes the genotyping platforms used.

claim: Samples were pre-phased using IMPUTE2 with no reference panel, then imputed into the 1000 Genomes Phase 1 reference panel.
source: Samples were pre-phased using IMPUTE2 (Howie et al., 2009) with no reference panel, then imputed into the 1000 Genomes Phase 1 reference panel (interim, data freeze, 10 November 2010, The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium 2012).
evidence: The manuscript describes the imputation procedure with citations.

claim: Post imputation, SNPs were removed if MAF < 0.01 or IMPUTE info value < 0.8.
source: Post imputation, SNPs were removed if MAF <0.01 or IMPUTE info value <0.8.
evidence: The manuscript describes quality control filters applied to imputed data.

claim: Samples were prepared for sequencing with the Illumina TruSeq sample preparation kit.
source: Samples were prepared for sequencing with the Illumina TruSeq sample preparation kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA) according to manufacturer's instructions and were sequenced on a HiSeq2000 machine.
evidence: The manuscript describes the RNA-seq library preparation method.

claim: 49-bp paired-end reads were mapped to the GRCh37 reference genome with BWA v0.5.9.
source: Afterwards, the 49-bp sequenced paired-end reads were mapped to the GRCh37 reference genome (The International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2001) with BWA v0.5.9 (Li and Durbin, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes the read mapping procedure with citations.

claim: Genes were defined as protein coding in the GENCODE 10 annotation.
source: We use genes defined as protein coding in the GENCODE 10 annotation (Harrow et al., 2012), removing genes with more than 10% zero read count.
evidence: The manuscript describes the gene annotation used with citation.

claim: Genes with more than 10% zero read count were removed.
source: We use genes defined as protein coding in the GENCODE 10 annotation (Harrow et al., 2012), removing genes with more than 10% zero read count.
evidence: The manuscript describes a quality control filter for gene expression.

claim: RPKM values were root mean transformed.
source: RPKM values were root mean transformed.
evidence: The manuscript describes the transformation applied to expression data.

claim: PEER software was used to remove 50 latent factors.
source: PEER software (Parts et al., 2011) was used to remove 50 latent factors; age and body mass index were included when factors were constructed, to prevent removal of important environmental factors.
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of PEER for confounder correction with citation.

claim: Age and body mass index were included when PEER factors were constructed to prevent removal of important environmental factors.
source: PEER software (Parts et al., 2011) was used to remove 50 latent factors; age and body mass index were included when factors were constructed, to prevent removal of important environmental factors.
evidence: The manuscript describes the rationale for including specific covariates in PEER analysis.

claim: Data were quantile normalised after PEER correction.
source: Data were then quantile normalised.
evidence: The manuscript describes the final normalization step.

claim: GRAMMAR was used to remove correlations between related individuals.
source: GRAMMAR (Aulchenko et al., 2007) was used to remove correlations between related individuals.
evidence: The manuscript describes the method used to account for relatedness with citation.

claim: Expression of each gene was tested against every SNP within 1 Mbp of the TSS.
source: Expression of each gene was tested against every SNP within 1 Mbp of the TSS.
evidence: The manuscript describes the cis window used for v-eQTL mapping.

claim: eQTL effects were removed by regressing expression on the posterior probability of being a heterozygote and the posterior probability of being a minor allele homozygote.
source: First, any eQTL effects were removed by regressing expression on the posterior probability of being a heterozygote and the posterior probability of being a minor allele homozygote.
evidence: The manuscript describes the procedure to remove mean effects before testing for variance effects.

claim: A Spearman rank correlation test between squared residuals and genotype dosage was used to assess evidence of variance effects.
source: The residuals were squared, giving a measure of distance from the mean expression of that genotype class for all individuals. A Spearman rank correlation test between this 'distance' and genotype dosage was used to assess evidence of variance effects.
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical test used for v-eQTL detection.

claim: A set of five permutations was applied to estimate the distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis.
source: A set of five permutations, consistent across all tests to consider linkage disequilibrium structure between SNPs, was applied to the distance residuals and the spearman correlation test was applied as before to estimate the distribution of the test statistic under the complete null hypothesis of no variance effects.
evidence: The manuscript describes the permutation procedure for significance testing.

claim: FDR was calculated as the proportion of permuted statistics more significant, divided by 5.
source: An FDR was calculated as the proportion of permuted statistics more significant, divided by 5.
evidence: The manuscript describes the FDR calculation method.

claim: The R package lme4 was used to fit linear mixed models using maximum likelihood to model expression as a function of genetic interactions.
source: The R package lme4 (Bolker, 2013) was used to fit linear mixed models using maximum likelihood to model expression as a function of genetic interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the software used for epistasis modeling with citation.

claim: A forward stepwise scheme was used to discover independent examples of epistasis.
source: A forward stepwise scheme, as used in Lappalainen et al. (2013) to map standard eQTL, was used to discover independent examples of epistasis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stepwise procedure for epistasis discovery with citation.

claim: A statistical test was applied to remove signals related to dominance.
source: A forward stepwise analysis identified independent examples of epistasis, not induced by linkage disequilibrium; a statistical test was applied to remove signals related to dominance ('Materials and methods').
evidence: The manuscript describes filtering to distinguish epistasis from dominance effects.

claim: Proportion of variance for linear mixed models was calculated as described in Nakagawa and Schielzeth (2012).
source: Proportion of variance for linear mixed models was calculated as described in Nakagawa and Schielzeth (2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites the method used to calculate variance explained.

claim: In the GEUVADIS replication, raw RPKM values were root transformed, 20 principal component factors were removed, and data were quantile normalised.
source: Raw RPKM values were root transformed, 20 principal component factors were removed and then the data were quantile normalised.
evidence: The manuscript describes the data processing for the replication cohort.

claim: Indicator variables for study population (CEU, YRI, TSI, GBR, FIN) were used to control for population effects in GEUVADIS.
source: Evidence for v-eQTL and epistasis was calculated as before, with indicator variables for study population (CEU, YRI, TSI, GBR, FIN) to control for population effects.
evidence: The manuscript describes how population structure was controlled in replication analysis.

claim: Of the 131 statistically significant interactions in GEUVADIS, 126 are also significant when log transformed data is analysed.
source: To ensure that our results are not caused by heteroskedasticity, we have considered various transformations to remove this issue and found the results to be robust. In particular, of the 131 statistically significant interactions in the GEUVADIS cohort, 126 are also significant when log transformed data is analysed (a typical way of accounting for heteroskedasticity).
evidence: The manuscript reports robustness analysis for heteroskedasticity.

claim: A forward stepwise cis eQTL scan reported all eQTL significant at p<10−5 in the GEUVADIS dataset.
source: To eliminate confounding with eQTL variants, an identical forward stepwise cis eQTL scan to that used in Lappalainen et al. (2013) reported all eQTL significant at p<10−5 in the GEUVADIS dataset.
evidence: The manuscript describes the eQTL mapping procedure used to rule out confounding.

claim: FDR was calculated using the qvalue package in R using default settings with lambda restricted to lie within the range of p values.
source: FDR was calculated using the qvalue package (Dabney and Storey, 2014) in R (R Development Core Team, 2008) using the default settings with the exception that lambda was restricted to lie within the range of the p values to prevent overly lenient correction.
evidence: The manuscript describes the FDR calculation method with citations.

claim: Segmentation analysis for LCL cell line GM12878 was downloaded from the UCSC website on 11/6/2013.
source: Segmentation analysis for LCL cell line GM12878 was downloaded from the UCSC website on 11/6/2013, url: http://hgdownload.cse.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg19/encodeDCC/wgEncodeBroadHmm/wgEncodeBroadHmmGm12878HMM.bed.gz.
evidence: The manuscript provides the source and date for ENCODE data used.

claim: Sequence data has been deposited at the European Genome-phenome Archive under accession number EGAS00001000805.
source: Sequence data has been deposited at the European Genome-phenome Archive (EGA, http://www.ebi.ac.uk/ega/) under accession number EGAS00001000805.
